meta.title: Who really said "Stumbling is not falling"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Malcolm X. A proverb collected in Haiti and printed in 1875, listed as Portuguese in 1950. The Malcolm X credit only appears in the 2000s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Stumbling is not falling'?
meta.ogDescription: A proverb, not a quotation. In English print by 1875 as a Haitian saying; this exact wording is filed as Portuguese in 1950. Malcolm X got the credit in the 2000s.

answer.label: Not Malcolm X — a proverb that long predates him
answer.authorDates: Traditional proverb · in English print by 1875
answer.sourceLine: This is a proverb, and proverbs do not have authors. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the earliest exact English match in Harper’s New Monthly Magazine for September 1875, in a collection of Haitian sayings gathered by John Bigelow: “A stumble is not a fall; or, One error is not ruin.” The precise wording quoted today appears in a 1950 proverb collection, filed under Portuguese. QI says Malcolm X received credit only in the 2000s — “which is very late” — and finds nothing to support it.

source.heading: Where the proverb actually comes from

docMeta.dd: John Bigelow, in ‘The Wit and Wisdom of the Haytians’
Racial Proverbs, ed. Selwyn Gurney Champion, 1950 — listed as Portuguese

source.excerpt: Butté pas tombé. — A stumble is not a fall; or, One error is not ruin.
trail: The earliest exact English match Quote Investigator locates ↗ is in Harper’s New Monthly Magazine for September 1875, in a series called ‘The Wit and Wisdom of the Haytians’ by John Bigelow. The proverb is given in Creole as ‘Butté pas tombé’ and rendered “A stumble is not a fall; or, One error is not ruin.” Bigelow was an American diplomat and editor who had spent time in Haiti collecting sayings who he was ↗.

The exact modern wording turns up in 1950, in Racial Proverbs: A Selection of the World’s Proverbs Arranged Linguistically, edited by Selwyn Gurney Champion — where “Stumbling is not falling.” is item 169 of the Portuguese section. QI also concludes the adage grew out of precursors in the 1600s and 1700s, so neither the Haitian nor the Portuguese filing is a claim of ultimate origin QI’s chronology ↗.

Against all of that, the Malcolm X credit is recent and unsupported. QI states plainly that he “received credit in the 2000s which is very late”, pointing to a 2005 newspaper item, and finds no historical evidence for it. Wikiquote’s Malcolm X page ↗ does not carry the line anywhere — it has no Misattributed or Disputed section at all, only sourced quotations and quotations about him.
source.cutTag: John Bigelow, 'The Wit and Wisdom of the Haytians', Harper's New Monthly Magazine, September 1875
source.excerptNote: The Creole and the English as Quote Investigator reproduces them from the 1875 magazine. The wording in circulation today — ‘Stumbling is not falling’ — is the form printed in Selwyn Gurney Champion’s Racial Proverbs in 1950, as item 169 of the Portuguese section. Two different collectors, two different languages, one very old idea.

source.rightsNote: We assert no rights status. A traditional proverb has no author to hold a copyright, and the 1875 Bigelow material is old enough to be free of United States copyright in any case — but the exact English wording on this page is one we can only trace to a 1950 compilation, and we have not established the status of that edition. Where the wording’s first printing is uncertain, we would rather claim nothing. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Malcolm X
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Malcolm X
author.metaLine: 1925–1965 · American Muslim minister and human-rights activist
author.bio: Malcolm X (born Malcolm Little, later el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz; 1925–1965) was an American Muslim minister and one of the most forceful orators of the civil-rights era, the Nation of Islam’s national spokesman before his break with it in 1964 and his assassination the following year. He is a heavy magnet for unsourced aphorisms because he genuinely produced short, hard, quotable sentences — so a compact maxim about perseverance sounds like him even when it is a Haitian proverb collected a half-century before he was born.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The line is quoted as Malcolm X almost everywhere online. The credit is about forty years younger than he is.

Wikiquote’s Malcolm X page collects his sourced quotations and has no Misattributed or Disputed section at all. This line does not appear on it in any form the page ↗.

items.who: A Haitian proverb, then a Portuguese one
items.why: Bigelow printed ‘Butté pas tombé’ — “A stumble is not a fall” — in Harper’s in September 1875, and Champion’s Racial Proverbs listed the exact modern wording among Portuguese sayings in 1950 the chronology ↗.

In a 2016 commencement address at Johnson C. Smith University she said “every stumble is not a fall, and every fall does not mean failure” — a variation on a proverb that was already in print long before QI on the 2016 speech ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: A proverb, not a quotation: in English print as a Haitian saying by 1875 and filed as Portuguese in 1950, decades before anyone attached Malcolm X’s name to it Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why proverbs get famous names
lead: A proverb has no owner, which makes it oddly unstable in a world of quotation graphics. An unattributed line looks unfinished; adding a famous name makes it shareable. So proverbs drift upward toward whoever the audience already admires.

Malcolm X is a natural destination for this one. The sentiment — a setback is not a defeat — sits close enough to what he actually said about struggle that nobody thinks to check, and the sentence is short enough to sound like oratory rather than folklore.
context.pull: An unattributed line looks unfinished. A famous name makes it shareable.
